subject: biology

items.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by integration in a living system?
items.correct: Coordination of the component parts so that together they perform an overall function that none performs alone.
items.misconception: Each component part performs its own function independently, so the parts do not need to interact.
items.why: Biology courses teach one system per chapter (digestive, circulatory, nervous), each with its own diagram, so students build a mental model of separate machines rather than of parts that only work through coordination. Coordination is needed for the component parts of a system to collectively perform an overall function. For example, the digestive system's absorbed glucose is useless to a muscle unless the circulatory system carries it there and the nervous system tells the muscle when to contract.
items.specStatementText: Parts of a living system must work together
items.random_wrong: A single dominant part carries out the overall function while the other parts play no role in it.

items.q: A cheetah can sprint at over 100 km per hour and catch fast-moving prey. Why is its effectiveness as a predator described as an emergent property?
items.correct: It arises from the integration of several body systems and is not a property of any one of them on its own.
items.misconception: It is a property of the muscular system alone, because the muscles are what make the cheetah run so fast.
items.why: Students are used to matching each function to one system ('muscles are for movement'), so when asked what makes the cheetah fast they name the system most obviously involved instead of the interaction between systems. An emergent property arises from the interaction of the parts and is not possessed by any part on its own. The cheetah becomes an effective predator by integration of its body systems: nervous control of the muscles, oxygen supplied by the respiratory and circulatory systems, and the skeleton acting as a system of levers.
items.specStatementText: Cells build tissues, organs and systems, and new properties emerge
items.random_wrong: It is a property already present in each of its muscle cells; the whole animal simply has many of them.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the roles of the nervous system and the endocrine system in sending messages between organs?
items.correct: Nervous messages travel as impulses along neurons to specific targets; hormones are carried by the blood to every organ.
items.misconception: Hormones are carried along nerves to their target organs, while nerve impulses are carried around the body in the blood plasma.
items.why: Students learn that epinephrine release is triggered by the nervous system and that the hypothalamus controls the pituitary, and they merge the two systems into a single set of 'wires' that carry every kind of message. The nervous system sends messages as electrical impulses along neurons; the endocrine system sends messages as hormones carried in the blood. Nerve fibres do not transport hormones. The two systems interact, for example at the hypothalamus, but they use different routes. Nerve fibres conduct impulses only; all materials, including hormones and glucose, are transported in the blood (C3.1.3).
items.specStatementText: Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
items.random_wrong: Both systems produce equally rapid responses that last equally long, and differ only in the chemical that carries the message.

items.q: After a meal, glucose absorbed in the small intestine is used for cell respiration in the leg muscles. How does the blood system integrate these two organs?
items.correct: Blood carries the glucose from capillaries in the intestine wall to the muscle cells.
items.misconception: The glucose passes to the muscles directly through the tissues, since blood only carries oxygen.
items.why: Blood is introduced through the respiratory system, red blood cells and oxygen, and the digestive system is taught separately with absorption as its end point, so students never connect absorbed nutrients with the circulation. The blood system integrates organs by transporting materials between them: glucose absorbed by the small intestine is carried to the liver and muscles, urea made by the liver is carried to the kidneys, and hormones are carried from glands to their targets, as well as oxygen from the lungs.
items.specStatementText: Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
items.random_wrong: Nerves running from the intestine to the leg muscles carry the glucose molecules along their fibres.

items.q: A tennis player watches the ball, hears it hit the opponent's racket, senses the position of her own arm and remembers where the opponent usually aims. What is the role of her brain in producing her return shot?
items.correct: It combines the information from all these inputs with stored memory and uses the result to decide the response.
items.misconception: It processes each input in its own region, and each region sends its own response to the muscles.
items.why: Brain maps labelled 'visual area', 'auditory area' and so on suggest independent modules, so students picture parallel channels rather than a central integrating organ. The brain is the central information integration organ: it processes information combined from several inputs, and uses learning and memory, before deciding on a response. Catching a ball uses sight, sound, the sense of body position and memory of previous catches together.
items.specStatementText: The brain combines inputs, learns and remembers
items.random_wrong: It only supplies timing, because the movement itself is stored in the arm muscles from previous practice.

items.q: Which statement about the spinal cord and unconscious processes is correct?
items.correct: The spinal cord integrates some unconscious responses, receiving sensory input and sending motor output without the brain deciding.
items.misconception: The spinal cord only conducts impulses between the body and the brain, so every kind of integration must take place in the brain itself.
items.why: Diagrams show the spinal cord as a thick white cord running down the back, like a wire, and the brain is introduced as 'the control centre', so students assume all processing must happen there. The spinal cord contains grey matter with interneurons and synapses, and it acts as an integrating centre for unconscious processes. In a pain reflex the sensory input is integrated in the spinal cord and the motor output sent without the brain making the decision.
items.specStatementText: The spinal cord integrates responses we are not aware of
items.random_wrong: Every unconscious process is integrated in the spinal cord, because everything that the brain does is conscious.

items.q: What is the function of sensory neurons?
items.correct: They convey impulses from receptor cells to the spinal cord and the cerebral hemispheres.
items.misconception: They carry impulses out from the central nervous system to the receptors that must then respond.
items.why: Students think of neurons as electrical wires, which conduct in either direction, and the labels 'sensory' and 'motor' are learned from a diagram rather than from the direction of travel. Input to the spinal cord and cerebral hemispheres is through sensory neurons; output to muscles is through motor neurons. The synapse makes transmission one-way, so two different neurons are needed for input and output.
items.specStatementText: Sensory neurons carry messages in
items.random_wrong: They detect every stimulus themselves, so the body needs no separate receptor cells.

items.q: A person decides to straighten their arm. How does output from the cerebral hemispheres produce this movement?
items.correct: Motor neurons stimulate the triceps to contract, and the biceps relaxes because it is no longer stimulated.
items.misconception: Epinephrine released into the blood stimulates the triceps to contract, because hormones control the skeletal muscles.
items.why: Epinephrine is described as preparing the body for 'fight or flight' and for 'vigorous activity', which students read as directly causing the vigorous activity. Muscles are stimulated to contract by motor neurons carrying output from the cerebral hemispheres. Epinephrine's role is to facilitate intense contraction by increasing the supply of oxygen and glucose to the muscles.
items.specStatementText: Motor neurons carry commands out to muscles
items.random_wrong: Motor neurons stimulate the triceps to contract and other motor neurons stimulate the biceps to lengthen actively.

items.q: A transverse section of a nerve shows an outer layer of connective tissue enclosing many small circular profiles. Some profiles have a thick pale ring around a central dot; others have no ring. What does the section show?
items.correct: A bundle of nerve fibres inside a protective sheath, the ringed profiles being myelinated fibres and the rest unmyelinated.
items.misconception: Several separate nerves, because the thick pale ring around each ringed profile is a nerve's protective sheath.
items.why: Both structures are called sheaths and both are described as protective or insulating, so students merge them into one. In a transverse section of a nerve, the outer protective sheath surrounds many nerve fibres. Inside it, myelinated fibres each have their own myelin sheath, formed by Schwann cells, while unmyelinated fibres have none.
items.specStatementText: A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
items.random_wrong: A bundle of fibres in which the profiles without a ring are damaged fibres that have lost their myelin.

items.q: Which statement about the relationship between a nerve and a neuron is correct?
items.correct: A nerve is a bundle of nerve fibres from many neurons and usually contains fibres of both sensory and motor neurons.
items.misconception: A nerve and a neuron are the same structure; nerve is simply the word used for a neuron long enough to be seen unaided.
items.why: The words are similar, everyday language uses 'nerve' for anything that carries signals, and the sciatic nerve and a motor neuron are both described as running from the spine to the leg. Nerves are bundles of nerve fibres of both sensory and motor neurons. A transverse section shows the protective sheath around many fibres, each belonging to a different neuron.
items.specStatementText: A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
items.random_wrong: A nerve contains the fibres of many neurons, but all the fibres in any one nerve are either sensory or motor.

items.q: A person touches a hot pan and withdraws their hand before feeling any pain. Which sequence describes the reflex arc that produced the withdrawal?
items.correct: free nerve ending → sensory neuron → interneuron in spinal cord grey matter → motor neuron → skeletal muscle of the arm
items.misconception: free nerve ending → sensory neuron → spinal cord → cerebral hemispheres → motor neuron → skeletal muscle of the arm
items.why: Everyday reasoning puts feeling before action ('it hurt, so I moved'), and the brain is presented as the organ that makes decisions, so students insert it into the reflex pathway. A pain reflex arc has a single interneuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord between the sensory neuron and the motor neuron. The response is involuntary and does not require the brain. Awareness of pain arises later, when impulses reach the cerebral hemispheres.
items.specStatementText: The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
items.random_wrong: free nerve ending → sensory neuron → interneuron in the spinal cord grey matter → motor neuron → smooth muscle of the arm

items.q: In the pain withdrawal reflex, the hand is pulled away before the person becomes aware of any pain. Which explanation accounts for this order of events?
items.correct: The reflex is completed in the spinal cord, and impulses giving awareness of pain reach the brain only later.
items.misconception: The arm muscle acts as the receptor as well as the effector, so it responds before the hand has sent any impulses at all.
items.why: The words receptor and effector are similar and are learned together as a pair, and the hand is both where the stimulus is detected and where the response is seen, so the two roles are conflated. A receptor detects a stimulus; an effector (a muscle or gland) carries out the response. In the pain reflex arc the receptor is a free nerve ending in a sensory neuron and the effector is skeletal muscle.
items.specStatementText: The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
items.random_wrong: The brain feels the pain first and decides to withdraw the hand, but this decision is made too fast to be noticed.

items.q: Which statement describes the role of the cerebellum in the control of body movements?
items.correct: It coordinates the contraction of skeletal muscles so that movements are smooth and accurate, and it maintains balance.
items.misconception: It initiates voluntary movements by deciding which skeletal muscles should contract and at what moment.
items.why: The cerebellum is summarized as 'controls movement and balance', and 'controls' is read as 'commands'. The cerebellum's role is in coordinating skeletal muscle contraction and balance: it adjusts the timing and strength of contractions commanded by the cerebral hemispheres. Damage to it makes movements clumsy and unsteady but does not prevent them being started.
items.specStatementText: The cerebellum makes movement smooth and keeps balance
items.random_wrong: It has no role in balance, which is maintained entirely by the semicircular canals within the inner ear.

items.q: Blood melatonin concentration in a person was measured over 24 hours. It was low from 08:00 to 20:00, rose from 21:00, was highest between 02:00 and 04:00 and had fallen by 07:00. Which statement explains this pattern and its effect?
items.correct: The pineal gland secretes melatonin while the eyes detect little light, and high melatonin at night promotes sleep.
items.misconception: Falling asleep stimulates the pineal gland to secrete melatonin, which is why the level rises after bedtime.
items.why: Students see melatonin described as 'the sleep hormone' and, noticing that it is high during sleep, reverse cause and effect. Melatonin secretion helps to establish the cycle of sleeping and waking. It rises in the evening as light fades, which promotes sleepiness, and stays high through the night; light in the morning suppresses it.
items.specStatementText: Melatonin from the pineal gland sets the sleep cycle
items.random_wrong: The pituitary gland secretes melatonin in response to darkness, and its high level makes the person sleepy.

items.q: A student who uses a bright screen until midnight finds it hard to fall asleep and wakes late the next morning. Using the role of melatonin in circadian rhythms, which explanation is best supported?
items.correct: Light from the screen suppresses evening melatonin secretion, delaying the rise that promotes sleep and shifting the cycle later.
items.misconception: Light from the screen stimulates melatonin secretion, and the high melatonin level keeps the student awake until it has all been used up.
items.why: Most hormones students meet are secreted in response to a stimulus that is present (glucose stimulates insulin), so they assume light is the stimulus for the 'daily' hormone rather than the signal that switches it off. The diurnal pattern of melatonin secretion by the pineal gland is the reverse: darkness allows secretion, light suppresses it. High melatonin at night promotes sleep, and the fall in melatonin in the morning is part of waking.
items.specStatementText: Melatonin from the pineal gland sets the sleep cycle
items.random_wrong: No melatonin was secreted because the student stayed awake, since the pineal gland only begins to secrete it once sleep has begun.

items.q: A sprinter waits for the starting signal and epinephrine is secreted into the blood. Which set of effects of epinephrine helps to facilitate intense contraction of the leg muscles during the race?
items.correct: Faster heart rate, wider bronchioles, glycogen breakdown in the liver and more blood flow to skeletal muscle.
items.misconception: Faster heart rate and an equal increase in blood flow to every organ, including the gut, the skin and the kidneys.
items.why: Students learn the increase in heart rate and cardiac output and reason that more output must mean more blood everywhere, without considering redistribution by changing the diameter of vessels. Among the widespread effects of epinephrine is the redistribution of blood: vasodilation in skeletal muscle and vasoconstriction in the digestive system and skin. This is one of the ways its effects facilitate intense muscle contraction.
items.specStatementText: Epinephrine readies the body for hard exercise
items.random_wrong: Direct transfer of energy from the adrenal glands to the leg muscle fibres, so that they can contract more strongly.

items.q: Which statement describes how the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland control the endocrine system?
items.correct: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland, which secretes hormones that act on body tissues or that control other endocrine glands.
items.misconception: The pituitary gland controls the other endocrine glands by itself; the hypothalamus is part of the nervous system and plays no role.
items.why: The phrase 'master gland' is widely used for the pituitary, and the hypothalamus is often introduced only as a brain region controlling temperature and thirst. The endocrine system is controlled by the hypothalamus and pituitary gland together: the hypothalamus controls the pituitary, and the pituitary secretes hormones that act on tissues or control other endocrine glands.
items.specStatementText: The hypothalamus runs the pituitary, which runs other glands
items.random_wrong: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary gland by nerve impulses only, because the hypothalamus cannot secrete any hormones.

items.q: Which statement gives the location and the function of the receptors that provide sensory input for the control of heart rate?
items.correct: Baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries monitor blood pressure; chemoreceptors there and in the medulla monitor pH, oxygen and carbon dioxide.
items.misconception: Baroreceptors and chemoreceptors are both in the wall of the heart, where they monitor the pressure and the chemistry of the blood as it passes through it.
items.why: Students reason that a system controlling the heart should have its sensors in the heart, and the heart is the only organ shown in most diagrams of heart rate control. Baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries monitor blood pressure, and chemoreceptors in the same arteries and in the medulla monitor blood pH, oxygen and carbon dioxide. They send impulses to the medulla, which sends nerve impulses to the heart.
items.specStatementText: Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
items.random_wrong: Baroreceptors in the aorta monitor blood pressure and chemoreceptors in the carotid arteries monitor only the concentration of oxygen.

items.q: A person stands up quickly and their blood pressure falls for a few seconds. Which sequence describes the feedback response that restores blood pressure?
items.correct: Baroreceptors in the arteries send fewer impulses to the medulla, which sends sympathetic impulses that raise heart rate and stroke volume.
items.misconception: Baroreceptors detect the fall and the medulla sends impulses along the vagus nerve to reduce heart rate, because a lower rate lets the pressure recover.
items.why: Students associate high blood pressure with strain and a racing heart, and they apply the epinephrine response (everything increases) to a situation that calls for the opposite correction. Control of heart rate is by negative feedback: a rise in blood pressure detected by baroreceptors leads the medulla to send impulses along the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve that reduce heart rate, lowering blood pressure. A fall in pressure leads to sympathetic impulses that increase heart rate and stroke volume.
items.specStatementText: Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
items.random_wrong: The medulla sends the impulses that cause each heartbeat more frequently, because the heart cannot beat at all unless the medulla drives it.

items.q: During a run, a student's blood carbon dioxide concentration rises, blood pH falls from 7.40 to 7.32 and ventilation rate rises from 12 to 30 breaths per minute. Which statement correctly links these changes?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, lowering pH; brainstem chemoreceptors detect this and the medulla increases signals to the breathing muscles.
items.misconception: The extra carbon dioxide makes the blood more alkaline, as shown by the fall in pH, and chemoreceptors in the brainstem respond to this by increasing ventilation.
items.why: The pH scale runs the opposite way to acidity, so students confuse 'higher pH' with 'more acid', and they do not connect carbon dioxide, a gas, with acid formation. Cell respiration produces carbon dioxide, which dissolves in plasma to form carbonic acid; the hydrogen ions released lower the pH (more acidic). This fall in pH is the change monitored by chemoreceptors in the brainstem.
items.specStatementText: Ventilation rate is adjusted by feedback from blood pH
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide is a gas and so cannot change pH; the fall in pH is due to lactic acid from the muscles, which is detected by chemoreceptors in the lungs.

items.q: A person swallows a mouthful of food. Which statement correctly describes how the movement of this food through the digestive system is controlled?
items.correct: Starting the swallow is voluntary and controlled by the CNS; peristalsis along the oesophagus and gut is involuntary and controlled by the ENS.
items.misconception: The CNS controls the whole process, sending an impulse to the gut muscles for each wave of peristalsis until faeces are egested.
items.why: Students learn that muscles contract when stimulated by motor neurons from the CNS, and they are not aware that the gut wall has its own nervous system. Only the initiation of swallowing and the egestion of faeces are under voluntary control by the CNS. Peristalsis between these points is under involuntary control by the enteric nervous system, which ensures the passage of material through the gut is coordinated.
items.specStatementText: Swallowing and egestion are voluntary; peristalsis in between is not
items.random_wrong: After swallowing, the food moves down the oesophagus and the intestine mainly under gravity, with muscle contraction only assisting.

items.q: Two students each measured the angle of curvature of the same seedling shoot five times with a protractor. Student A recorded 28°, 29°, 28°, 29°, 28°. Student B recorded 22°, 35°, 30°, 26°, 37°. A later check showed that the true angle was 35° and that Student A had aligned the protractor with the edge of the pot instead of the vertical part of the stem. Which conclusion is justified?
items.correct: Student A's measurements are precise but not accurate, because a systematic error shifted all of them away from the true value.
items.misconception: Student A's measurements are both precise and accurate, because five repeats that agree so closely must lie close to the true value.
items.why: In everyday language 'precise' and 'accurate' are synonyms, and students rarely have an independent true value to compare against, so they judge accuracy by consistency. Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to each other; accuracy is the closeness of a measurement to the true value. A systematic error reduces accuracy without reducing precision.
items.specStatementText: Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
items.random_wrong: Student A could have obtained an accurate mean by taking more repeats, because repetition removes systematic error.

items.q: Students investigating phototropism recorded three observations of seedlings lit from one side: (1) a labelled drawing showing the shoot curved towards the lamp; (2) 'the shoots bent much more than those of the control'; (3) an angle of curvature of 32° measured with a protractor. Which classification is correct?
items.correct: (1) and (2) are qualitative observations and (3) is a quantitative observation.
items.misconception: (2) and (3) are quantitative because both describe the amount of bending; (1) is qualitative.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'quality' is 'how good', so students attach the terms to how good the data seem rather than to whether a quantity was measured. A diagram of a curved seedling and the statement 'the shoot bent more than the control' are qualitative observations. A measured angle of curvature is a quantitative observation, whether or not the repeats vary.
items.specStatementText: Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
items.random_wrong: Only (3) is an observation; (1) and (2) are not data as they have no number.

items.q: A seedling is grown in a box with a window on its left side only. After two days the shoot has curved towards the window. Which statement explains the curvature?
items.correct: Cells on the shaded right side elongated more than cells on the lit left side, so growth bent the shoot to the left.
items.misconception: Cells on the lit left side elongated more because the light supplied the energy for their growth, pulling the shoot over.
items.why: Students know that light drives photosynthesis and that plants 'grow towards light', so they conclude that growth happens where the light is. Positive phototropism is a directional growth response in which the shaded side elongates more than the lit side. Growth towards the light is produced by faster elongation on the side away from it.
items.specStatementText: Shoots grow towards light from the side
items.random_wrong: The existing tissues of the shoot bent towards the window in the way an animal turns its head, without any growth occurring.

items.q: Which statement about phytohormones is correct?
items.correct: Plants use a variety of chemicals, including auxins, cytokinins and ethylene, as signals controlling growth, development and responses to stimuli.
items.misconception: Auxin is the only phytohormone, and all plant growth, development and responses to stimuli are controlled by its concentration.
items.why: Auxin is the phytohormone taught in most detail (phototropism, efflux carriers, cell elongation), so it comes to stand for all plant signalling. Students should appreciate that a variety of chemicals are used as phytohormones. Cytokinin interacts with auxin to integrate root and shoot growth, and the gas ethylene controls fruit ripening.
items.specStatementText: Plants signal with a variety of chemicals
items.random_wrong: Phytohormones are secreted by glands in the plant and carried in the xylem to all parts, just as animal hormones are carried in blood.

items.q: In a column of cells in a shoot, every cell has its auxin efflux carriers concentrated in the membrane at its lower (basal) end. What happens to auxin in this tissue?
items.correct: Auxin enters each cell freely by diffusion but can leave only through the basal carriers, so it is transported downwards and accumulates below.
items.misconception: The efflux carriers pump auxin into each cell from the cell below, so auxin is transported upwards and accumulates at the shoot tip.
items.why: The prefix 'ef-' is unfamiliar, and students expect a carrier to be needed for entry, since entry is what carriers do in most transport examples they have met. Auxin diffuses freely into cells and needs no carrier to enter. Auxin efflux carriers pump it out, and their position on one side of each cell produces one-directional transport through the tissue.
items.specStatementText: Efflux carriers push auxin one way through a tissue
items.random_wrong: Auxin diffuses in and out of every cell across all parts of its membrane, so the carriers make no difference and the auxin stays evenly spread throughout.

items.q: Which statement describes how auxin promotes the elongation of a plant cell?
items.correct: It promotes hydrogen ion secretion into the apoplast; the acidified wall has its cellulose cross links loosened and can stretch.
items.misconception: It stimulates the cell to divide by mitosis, so the tissue becomes longer because it contains a larger number of cells.
items.why: Growth is introduced in earlier courses as cell division, so any hormone that 'promotes growth' is assumed to promote division. Auxin's promotion of cell growth is through elongation. It promotes hydrogen ion secretion into the apoplast, acidifying the cell wall and loosening cross links between cellulose molecules, which facilitates cell elongation.
items.specStatementText: Auxin loosens cell walls so cells elongate
items.random_wrong: It stimulates secretion of hydrogen ions into the cell wall, where the acid dissolves the cellulose molecules so the wall can be rebuilt longer.

items.q: A plant's roots are damaged, reducing the number of root tips. Using the interaction between auxin and cytokinin, what is the predicted effect on the shoots?
items.correct: Less cytokinin reaches the shoots, so shoot growth is reduced to match the smaller root system.
items.misconception: Less auxin is transported to the shoots, because root tips are where auxin is produced, so shoot growth is reduced.
items.why: Students associate auxin with roots because of its commercial use in rooting powder, and the two names and sources are learned as a pair that is easily swapped. Root tips produce cytokinin, which is transported to shoots, and shoot tips produce auxin, which is transported to roots. This exchange of signals is what integrates root and shoot growth.
items.specStatementText: Root and shoot tips signal to each other
items.random_wrong: Shoot growth is unaffected, because cytokinin acts only in the roots where it is made, and auxin only in the shoots.

items.q: The concentration of ethylene in the air around a ripening fruit was measured each day: 0.1, 0.3, 1.2 and 4.8 ppm on days 1 to 4, by which time the fruit was fully ripe. Which statement best interprets these data?
items.correct: Ethylene stimulates ripening and ripening stimulates more ethylene production, so the concentration rises faster and faster: positive feedback.
items.misconception: Ethylene production is under negative feedback, so each rise in ethylene reduces further production and ripening proceeds steadily.
items.why: Almost every control system students meet (blood glucose, body temperature, heart rate) is negative feedback, so they assume all feedback in biology stabilizes a variable. Ethylene stimulates the changes in fruits that occur during ripening, and ripening also stimulates increased production of ethylene. This positive feedback ensures that ripening is rapid and synchronized.
items.specStatementText: Ethylene and ripening drive each other
items.random_wrong: The mechanism is positive feedback because ripening benefits the plant; a harmful process with this pattern would be negative feedback.

items.q: Why is positive feedback in ethylene production beneficial to a plant?
items.correct: It makes ripening rapid and synchronized, so the fruits on the plant become attractive to seed-dispersing animals together.
items.misconception: Positive feedback is, by definition, feedback that benefits the organism, so its benefit to the plant needs no further explanation.
items.why: In everyday language 'positive' and 'negative' feedback mean praise and criticism, and students transfer these value meanings to the biological terms. In fruit ripening, positive feedback (ethylene increases ripening, which increases ethylene) is beneficial because it makes ripening rapid and synchronized; but the term describes the direction of the effect, not its value.
items.specStatementText: Ethylene and ripening drive each other
items.random_wrong: It keeps the rate of ripening slow and steady, so the plant is not left with more ripe fruit than can be dispersed.

items.q: Are the properties of a tissue, organ or organism simply the properties of its cells, scaled up?
items.correct: No. Each level of the hierarchy has emergent properties that its component parts do not have; they arise from the interaction between the parts.
items.misconception: Everything an organ or organism can do is already present in its individual cells; the whole is just many copies of the same ability.
items.why: Cell theory is taught as 'cells are the basic unit of life' and students take this to mean that all the properties of life reside in single cells, so they see higher levels as containers rather than as systems with new properties. Cells, tissues, organs and body systems form a hierarchy of subsystems, and the integration of each level produces emergent properties. A single muscle cell cannot run; running emerges from the coordinated activity of muscles, skeleton, nerves, blood and lungs.
items.specStatementText: Cells build tissues, organs and systems, and new properties emerge
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a hormone delivered only to its target organ?
items.correct: No. The blood carries a hormone to every part of the body; only cells with receptors for that hormone respond to it.
items.misconception: The blood carries each hormone specifically to its target organ, in the same way that a nerve leads to one particular target.
items.why: Diagrams draw an arrow from the gland to the target organ, and the word 'target' suggests aiming, so students imagine the hormone being sent somewhere rather than everywhere. Hormones are distributed by the blood throughout the body. Specificity comes from the target cells, which have receptors for the hormone, not from the route. This is one reason a hormone such as epinephrine can affect many organs at once, whereas a nerve impulse reaches only the cells its neuron connects to.
items.specStatementText: Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do hormonal responses happen as quickly as nervous responses?
items.correct: No. Nerve impulses produce responses within milliseconds; hormonal responses are typically slower to start and last longer, because the hormone must be secreted, carried in the blood and bind to receptors.
items.misconception: The two systems are interchangeable ways of sending instant messages; they differ only in the chemical used.
items.why: The everyday phrase 'adrenaline rush' makes hormone action seem instantaneous, and students who learn that both systems 'send messages' assume the messages travel at the same speed. The roles of the two systems differ: the nervous system gives fast, precisely targeted, short-lived responses along fixed pathways; the endocrine system gives slower, more widespread and longer-lasting responses through hormones in the blood.
items.specStatementText: Nerves, hormones and blood link organs together
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where is a learned skill such as a tennis serve stored?
items.correct: In the brain. Learning and memory are functions of the brain; the muscles themselves store nothing.
items.misconception: 'Muscle memory' means that practised movements are stored in the muscles, so the brain is not needed to reproduce them.
items.why: The everyday phrase 'muscle memory' is taken literally, and students notice that skilled movements happen without conscious thought, which they equate with the brain not being involved. The brain's role includes learning and memory. A practised movement becomes automatic because the brain has stored a refined motor programme, not because the muscles have learned it. Skeletal muscle only contracts when it is stimulated by motor neurons carrying output from the brain.
items.specStatementText: The brain combines inputs, learns and remembers
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is everything the brain does conscious?
items.correct: No. Much of the brain's activity is unconscious, such as the medulla's control of heart rate and ventilation and the cerebellum's coordination of movement.
items.misconception: The brain is the organ of conscious thought, so any process that does not involve conscious decision must be handled outside the brain, in the spinal cord.
items.why: The spinal cord is introduced as the integrating centre for unconscious processes and the cerebral hemispheres for conscious ones, and students extend 'cerebral hemispheres' to 'the whole brain'. Conscious processes involve the cerebral hemispheres. Unconscious processes are integrated either in the spinal cord (reflexes) or in parts of the brain such as the medulla and cerebellum. The distinction is between conscious and unconscious processing, not between brain and spinal cord.
items.specStatementText: The spinal cord integrates responses we are not aware of
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a sensory neuron the same thing as a receptor?
items.correct: Not in general. In most sense organs separate receptor cells detect the stimulus and pass a signal to the sensory neuron; only in some cases, such as the free nerve endings that detect pain, is the ending of the sensory neuron itself the receptor.
items.misconception: Every sensory neuron detects its stimulus directly, so the body has no receptor cells other than sensory neurons.
items.why: The pain reflex arc, which is the example every student learns, has a free nerve ending acting as the receptor, so students generalize it to all senses. Sensory neurons convey messages from receptor cells to the central nervous system. Photoreceptor cells in the retina and hair cells in the cochlea are receptor cells that are not neurons; they signal to sensory neurons. The free nerve ending of a pain receptor is a special case.
items.specStatementText: Sensory neurons carry messages in
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a nerve carry impulses in one direction only?
items.correct: No. A typical nerve contains fibres of both sensory and motor neurons, so impulses travel towards the CNS in some fibres and away from it in others.
items.misconception: Each nerve is either a sensory nerve or a motor nerve, so all its fibres carry impulses the same way.
items.why: Reflex arc diagrams label a 'sensory neuron' and a 'motor neuron' as two separate lines, and students assume the nerves of the body are sorted in the same way. Nerves are bundles of nerve fibres of both sensory and motor neurons. The direction of conduction is a property of each individual neuron, not of the nerve as a whole.
items.specStatementText: A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are unmyelinated nerve fibres abnormal?
items.correct: No. Healthy nerves normally contain both myelinated and unmyelinated fibres; unmyelinated fibres simply conduct more slowly.
items.misconception: All normal nerve fibres are myelinated, so a fibre without myelin must be damaged or diseased.
items.why: Every diagram of a neuron shows a myelin sheath, and the only context in which students hear of fibres lacking myelin is disease such as multiple sclerosis. A transverse section of a nerve shows both myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibres within the same protective sheath. Many sensory fibres, including those carrying slow pain, are unmyelinated in health.
items.specStatementText: A nerve is a bundle of many fibres
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which type of muscle is the effector in the pain withdrawal reflex?
items.correct: Skeletal muscle. Although the response is involuntary, the muscles that move the arm are skeletal muscles.
items.misconception: Because skeletal muscle is 'voluntary muscle', an involuntary response such as a reflex must use smooth muscle.
items.why: Muscle types are introduced as 'voluntary' (skeletal) and 'involuntary' (smooth, cardiac), so students match the type of muscle to whether the response was chosen rather than to the muscle's location. Pain reflex arcs are involuntary responses with skeletal muscle as the effector. Whether a response is voluntary depends on whether the cerebral hemispheres initiate it, not on the type of muscle that contracts.
items.specStatementText: The pain reflex withdraws the hand before you feel it
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is balance maintained by the inner ear alone?
items.correct: No. The inner ear provides sensory information, but balance is maintained by the cerebellum, which integrates this with information from the eyes and from muscles and joints and adjusts muscle contraction.
items.misconception: Balance is entirely a function of the semicircular canals of the inner ear, with no involvement of the brain.
items.why: The ear is taught as 'the organ of hearing and balance', which students take to mean that the ear itself keeps the body balanced rather than merely detecting movement. Receptors detect; the cerebellum integrates and coordinates. The cerebellum's role includes maintaining balance and posture by coordinating skeletal muscle contraction in response to sensory input.
items.specStatementText: The cerebellum makes movement smooth and keeps balance
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the cerebellum control the heartbeat and breathing?
items.correct: No. Those involuntary processes are coordinated by the medulla of the brainstem. The cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle contraction and balance.
items.misconception: The cerebellum is the part of the brain that controls involuntary processes such as heart rate and breathing.
items.why: The cerebellum and the medulla are both at the back and base of the brain, both are described as controlling processes 'without conscious thought', and 'cerebellum' is the more memorable name. The cerebellum coordinates skeletal muscle contraction and balance. Heart rate and ventilation rate are controlled by the medulla, which receives input from baroreceptors and chemoreceptors.
items.specStatementText: The cerebellum makes movement smooth and keeps balance
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which gland secretes melatonin?
items.correct: The pineal gland, in the brain.
items.misconception: Melatonin is secreted by the pituitary gland, since the pituitary is the master gland that produces the body's hormones.
items.why: The pituitary is the gland students know as being in the brain and as controlling the endocrine system, so any hormone 'from the brain' is attributed to it. Melatonin is secreted by the pineal gland in a diurnal pattern, with high secretion at night. The pituitary is a different gland with different hormones.
items.specStatementText: Melatonin from the pineal gland sets the sleep cycle
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does epinephrine supply energy to muscles?
items.correct: No. Epinephrine is a signal. It increases the supply of glucose and oxygen to muscles and makes the heart pump faster; the energy for contraction comes from cell respiration in the muscle.
items.misconception: An 'adrenaline rush' is a burst of energy delivered by the hormone itself to the muscles.
items.why: The everyday phrase 'adrenaline rush' and descriptions of adrenaline 'giving you energy' make the hormone sound like a fuel rather than a messenger. Epinephrine prepares the body for vigorous activity through widespread effects: increased heart rate and stroke volume, dilated bronchioles, breakdown of liver glycogen raising blood glucose, and diversion of blood to skeletal muscle. These effects facilitate intense muscle contraction by supplying the muscles with more glucose and oxygen for cell respiration.
items.specStatementText: Epinephrine readies the body for hard exercise
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the hypothalamus secrete hormones?
items.correct: Yes. Although it is part of the brain, the hypothalamus produces hormones, some of which control the secretion of hormones by the pituitary gland.
items.misconception: The hypothalamus is purely a nervous structure and cannot secrete any hormones, so it can only control the pituitary by nerve impulses.
items.why: The hypothalamus is part of the brain, and students have learned that the brain sends messages as nerve impulses and glands send messages as hormones, so a brain region that secretes hormones does not fit either category. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems. It monitors the blood and receives nervous input, and it controls the pituitary gland, including by means of hormones that it produces itself.
items.specStatementText: The hypothalamus runs the pituitary, which runs other glands
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do endocrine glands such as the thyroid gland and the gonads act independently?
items.correct: No. Their secretion is controlled by hormones from the pituitary gland, which is in turn controlled by the hypothalamus.
items.misconception: Each endocrine gland monitors the blood and decides for itself when to secrete its hormone; no gland controls another.
items.why: The glands students meet first (the pancreas secreting insulin in response to blood glucose) do respond directly to the blood, and this pattern is generalized to every gland. Control of the endocrine system is exercised by the hypothalamus and pituitary gland. Several pituitary hormones act on other endocrine glands and control their secretion, so the endocrine system is integrated rather than a set of independent glands.
items.specStatementText: The hypothalamus runs the pituitary, which runs other glands
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the medulla cause each heartbeat?
items.correct: No. The heart beats on its own initiative; the medulla sends impulses along the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves to speed the heart up or slow it down and to change its stroke volume.
items.misconception: The medulla sends the impulses that make the heart beat, so without these impulses the heart would stop.
items.why: Students learn that the medulla 'controls the heart' and that muscles contract when stimulated by nerves, so they assume cardiac muscle needs a nerve impulse for every contraction. The role of the medulla is to coordinate responses to input from baroreceptors and chemoreceptors and to send nerve impulses to the heart that change the heart's rate and stroke volume. The nerves modulate a rhythm the heart generates itself.
items.specStatementText: Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are blood pressure receptors located in the brain?
items.correct: No. Baroreceptors are in the walls of the aorta and the carotid arteries. The medulla in the brain receives their impulses; it contains chemoreceptors but not baroreceptors.
items.misconception: The medulla itself senses blood pressure, so the baroreceptors are located in the brain.
items.why: The medulla is the centre that responds to blood pressure, and students who learn that some chemoreceptors are in the medulla assume the pressure sensors are there too. Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the artery walls where they can detect changes in pressure directly; the medulla is the coordinating centre, not the sensor.
items.specStatementText: Heart rate is adjusted by feedback from pressure and chemical sensors
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which change in the blood is the main stimulus for increasing ventilation rate?
items.correct: A rise in carbon dioxide concentration, which lowers blood pH; chemoreceptors detect the pH change. Oxygen concentration is also monitored but is not the main stimulus.
items.misconception: Breathing speeds up because the body detects that it is running short of oxygen; carbon dioxide is not sensed.
items.why: Students know that the purpose of breathing is to obtain oxygen, so they assume oxygen shortage is what is sensed, and carbon dioxide is thought of only as waste. Chemoreceptors monitor blood pH and the concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. During exercise the rise in carbon dioxide and the resulting fall in pH are detected by chemoreceptors in the brainstem and lead to an increase in ventilation rate.
items.specStatementText: Ventilation rate is adjusted by feedback from blood pH
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ventilation rate under voluntary control?
items.correct: Normally no. Ventilation rate is controlled unconsciously by the medulla in response to chemoreceptor input; conscious control can override it only briefly.
items.misconception: We breathe faster during exercise because we decide to; breathing is a voluntary action.
items.why: Everyone can hold their breath or breathe deliberately, so students conclude that breathing is normally under conscious control. Chemoreceptors in the brainstem monitor blood pH and the medulla sends signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, increasing ventilation rate automatically when carbon dioxide rises. Voluntary control is temporary: the chemoreceptor drive eventually forces breathing to resume.
items.specStatementText: Ventilation rate is adjusted by feedback from blood pH
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can carbon dioxide, a gas, change the pH of the blood?
items.correct: Yes. Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which lowers blood pH. This is the usual cause of the fall in pH during exercise.
items.misconception: A gas cannot be an acid, so the only substance that lowers blood pH during exercise is lactic acid.
items.why: Lactic acid is the acid students associate with exercise, and carbon dioxide is thought of as an inert waste gas rather than as something that reacts with water. The causes of pH changes in the blood include carbon dioxide from cell respiration forming carbonic acid, as well as lactic acid from anaerobic respiration. The carbon dioxide effect operates in all exercise and is detected by chemoreceptors in the brainstem.
items.specStatementText: Ventilation rate is adjusted by feedback from blood pH
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does food move through the gut by gravity?
items.correct: No. It is moved by peristalsis, waves of muscle contraction in the gut wall, which work in any orientation.
items.misconception: Food falls down the oesophagus and through the intestine under gravity, with muscle contraction only helping it along.
items.why: Everyday language ('food goes down') and the vertical orientation of the digestive system in diagrams suggest that gravity does the work. Peristalsis is coordinated by the enteric nervous system and moves material along the gut independently of gravity; a person can swallow while lying down or upside down.
items.specStatementText: Swallowing and egestion are voluntary; peristalsis in between is not
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is swallowing entirely involuntary?
items.correct: No. The initiation of swallowing is voluntary and under control of the CNS; the subsequent peristalsis is involuntary.
items.misconception: Swallowing is a reflex from start to finish, so no part of the passage of food is under voluntary control.
items.why: Swallowing is often described as a reflex, and students notice that once started it cannot be stopped, so they overlook the voluntary decision that starts it. Initiation of swallowing of food and egestion of faeces are under voluntary control by the CNS. Between these points, peristalsis is under involuntary control by the enteric nervous system.
items.specStatementText: Swallowing and egestion are voluntary; peristalsis in between is not
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does repeating a measurement more times make it more accurate?
items.correct: Repeats reduce the effect of random error and improve reliability, but they do not remove a systematic error, so they do not by themselves make a measurement accurate.
items.misconception: Taking more repeats corrects every kind of error, so a large enough number of repeats guarantees an accurate mean.
items.why: 'Repeat and take a mean' is taught as the general remedy for error, without distinguishing random error (which averages out) from systematic error (which does not). Strategies for increasing precision and reliability include repeats and larger samples. Accuracy is improved by removing systematic error: calibrating the instrument, aligning the protractor correctly, or measuring from a photograph.
items.specStatementText: Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are drawings and descriptions of seedlings valid scientific data?
items.correct: Yes. Qualitative observations recorded as annotated diagrams are valid data; they record features such as the direction of curvature that a single angle measurement does not.
items.misconception: Only numerical measurements count as data; drawings and written descriptions are not real observations.
items.why: Assessment rewards tables and graphs of numbers, so students come to regard anything without a number as unscientific. Students should gather qualitative data, using diagrams to record their observations of seedlings, and may also collect quantitative data by measuring the angle of curvature. Both kinds of observation are used in science.
items.specStatementText: Recording tropisms: diagrams and angles
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is phototropism a movement of the shoot, like an animal turning towards something?
items.correct: No. It is a growth response: cells on one side elongate more than cells on the other, so new growth is directed towards the light.
items.misconception: The shoot bends towards the light by moving its existing tissues, and can bend back again if the light moves, without any growth.
items.why: Time-lapse films make shoots appear to 'turn', and the sunflower's daily tracking of the sun is a familiar image, so students think of tropism as motion rather than as directed growth. A tropism is a directional growth response. Positive phototropism of shoots is caused by differential elongation of cells on the two sides of the shoot and takes hours to days.
items.specStatementText: Shoots grow towards light from the side
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are phytohormones produced by glands and carried in a transport system like animal hormones in blood?
items.correct: No. Plants have no glands. Phytohormones are produced by cells in many tissues and move from cell to cell or in the xylem and phloem.
items.misconception: Plants have hormone-producing glands and a circulatory system that carries every phytohormone to all parts of the plant.
items.why: Students learn animal hormones first and transfer the whole model, gland and bloodstream included, to plants. Phytohormones are signalling chemicals produced in plant tissues such as shoot tips and root tips. Some, like auxin, are transported from cell to cell by carriers, which allows concentration gradients to be set up within a tissue.
items.specStatementText: Plants signal with a variety of chemicals
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the acid in the cell wall dissolve the cellulose?
items.correct: No. The low pH loosens the cross links between cellulose molecules so that the wall can stretch; the cellulose molecules themselves remain intact.
items.misconception: Acidifying the cell wall breaks down or dissolves the cellulose fibres, and the wall is then rebuilt at a larger size.
items.why: Students associate acid with corrosion and digestion, so 'acidifying the wall' is heard as 'dissolving the wall'. Auxin-induced acidification of the apoplast loosens the cross links between cellulose molecules, allowing them to slide past each other as the cell takes up water and elongates. The cellulose is not broken down.
items.specStatementText: Auxin loosens cell walls so cells elongate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is there more auxin on the shaded side of a shoot lit from one side?
items.correct: Because auxin is transported laterally, by efflux carriers, from the lit side to the shaded side. The total amount of auxin is unchanged.
items.misconception: Light destroys the auxin on the lit side, so the shaded side has more only because its auxin survived.
items.why: The idea that light 'breaks down' auxin is an appealing explanation that once had scientific supporters, and it avoids needing to understand carrier positioning. Concentration gradients of auxin are set up by auxin efflux carriers that move auxin towards the shaded side. Experiments show the total auxin in a lit shoot equals that in a dark shoot; it is redistributed, not destroyed.
items.specStatementText: Auxin loosens cell walls so cells elongate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where does auxin cause the hydrogen ions to accumulate?
items.correct: In the apoplast, the cell wall outside the plasma membrane. The cytoplasm is not acidified.
items.misconception: Auxin acidifies the cytoplasm, and the acidic cell contents draw in water by osmosis to enlarge the cell.
items.why: Students associate chemical changes with the inside of the cell, and cell enlargement with osmotic water uptake, so they place the acid where they expect the action to be. Auxin promotes secretion of hydrogen ions from the cytoplasm into the apoplast, so it is the wall, not the cytoplasm, that becomes acidic. The loosened wall then allows the cell to elongate as it takes up water.
items.specStatementText: Auxin loosens cell walls so cells elongate
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do auxin and cytokinin act only where they are produced?
items.correct: No. Each is transported to the other organ: auxin to the roots and cytokinin to the shoots, so that the growth of each organ is influenced by the other.
items.misconception: Auxin controls the shoot where it is made and cytokinin controls the root where it is made; the two hormones do not interact.
items.why: Students expect a hormone to act locally, and they have not seen why a plant would need the roots and shoots to inform each other. Interactions between auxin and cytokinin help to ensure that root and shoot growth are integrated. Because each organ's hormone is transported to the other, a plant with fewer root tips sends less cytokinin to its shoots, and shoot growth is restrained to match.
items.specStatementText: Root and shoot tips signal to each other
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can the ethylene from one fruit affect other fruits?
items.correct: Yes. Ethylene is a gas that diffuses through the air, so a ripening fruit stimulates ripening in neighbouring fruits.
items.misconception: Ethylene acts only within the fruit that produces it, so the ripening of one fruit cannot affect another.
items.why: Hormones are learned as substances carried inside an organism, so students do not expect a hormone to leave the plant and act on another fruit through the air. Ethylene (ethene) is gaseous. Its diffusion between fruits is part of why positive feedback produces synchronized ripening of the fruits on a plant, and why one ripe fruit in a container hastens the ripening of the rest.
items.specStatementText: Ethylene and ripening drive each other
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
